claims.text: A product is the good or service offered to meet a customer need. It includes relevant features, quality, design and supporting service rather than only a physical object. A repair service is a product offering even though the customer is not simply buying a newly manufactured item. Product is distinct from production, the process of creating the offering. Customers judge whether benefits meet their purpose at an acceptable price. A technically impressive feature may add cost without value if buyers do not need it.

claims.text: A product life cycle describes the stages a product passes through from introduction, through growth and maturity, and finally decline. It is a model of sales through time, not a promise of identical timing for every product. Introduction commonly involves low initial sales and awareness-building; growth brings rising sales; maturity involves slower growth or a plateau; decline involves falling sales. Development can precede introduction, but sales have not yet begun. Managers can use evidence to consider changes, while recognising a temporary fall does not prove permanent decline.

claims.text: Put time on the horizontal axis and sales on the vertical axis. Draw low introductory sales, a rising growth section, a high flatter maturity section and a declining section. The curve is conceptual unless data are supplied; do not present it as actual measured sales or assume a given number of years per stage. Extension actions such as adapting the product or finding new buyers can sometimes prolong sales but do not guarantee revival.

claims.text: Cost-plus pricing adds a mark-up to a relevant unit-cost base. Penetration sets a low initial price to encourage market entry and customer trial. Skimming sets a high initial price for a distinctive new offering where some buyers will pay, often reducing it later. Competitive pricing uses rivals’ prices as a reference. Promotional pricing makes a temporary price reduction or special offer. Choose according to objectives, demand, competition, costs, product and capacity. A strategy is a pricing approach, not proof of customer response. A low price cannot compensate for an unwanted or unavailable product.

claims.text: For cost-plus pricing, calculate the mark-up on the stated cost and add it to that cost. A mark-up on cost is different from a profit margin on sales. For a promotional percentage reduction, calculate the reduction on the original selling price and subtract it. State the base, currency and final price. A discount on a cost-plus price is applied to the resulting selling price, not silently to the original cost. The final price must still be assessed against demand and relevant costs; arithmetic alone does not establish a good strategy.

claims.text: Fictional Luma Cases has full unit cost N$80 and applies a 25% mark-up on cost, then offers 10% off that selling price. Mark-up = 80 × 0.25 = N$20. Normal price = 80 + 20 = N$100. claims.text: Fictional Tula Tools can make a small reliable range of durable tool bags for local tradespeople. Full unit cost is N$80 and research supports testing a price of N$120. The owner has limited promotion funds and can supply by workshop collection. Original plan: target local tradespeople needing durable organised storage; objective—test paid demand and repeat interest over four weeks within current capacity. Product—durable tool bag with practical compartments and clear care information. Price—test N$120 against N$80 stated unit cost, review actual uptake and costs. Promotion—local demonstration and a concise accessible notice explaining the benefit and collection arrangements. Distribution—direct workshop collection, recording orders to avoid exceeding capacity. Action/review—owner confirms material supply, schedules a small trial, records paid units and feedback weekly and revises the offer before expansion. This is a connected plan, not four unrelated definitions.
